title: Stored procedures
one: One procedure per action: the only way your program touches the data.
marks: This chapter is where the examiner looks for every add, change, delete and search going through a stored procedure, with the database saying no in a sentence when a rule would be broken.

screens.title: Read what a stored procedure is, and why every action gets one.

blocks.p: In chapter 3 you typed SELECT, INSERT and DELETE lines into a query window and ran them yourself. Your program cannot do that. A program needs each action it takes on the data to be written down once, given a name, and kept inside the database, so that the program only has to say the name. That is a stored procedure: a recipe with a name, saved in the database. The program says the name and hands over the ingredients, such as a customer's name and phone number, and the database does the rest.

Every action your program will ever take on the data gets its own stored procedure: search for customers, fetch one customer, add one, change one, delete one, and so on. The program never sends a SELECT or an INSERT of its own. That is the rule. The top mark band asks for a program that adds, deletes, changes and displays related data from more than one table, and marking last year's work showed that doing every one of those through a stored procedure is what the examiner expects to see.

There is one more reason. A stored procedure can check before it acts. If the shop tries to delete a customer who has bookings, the stored procedure says no, in a sentence, and the program shows that sentence. The rule lives in the database, so no screen can forget it. By the end of this chapter you will have fifteen stored procedures in your script, and the first refusal.

words: Stored procedure
A recipe with a name, saved inside the database, that the program runs by saying the name.
Parameter
One ingredient a stored procedure needs, such as a customer's first name, with a name that starts with @.
EXEC
The word that runs a stored procedure by name, handing over the parameters it needs.
OUTPUT
A parameter that carries an answer back out of the stored procedure, instead of carrying a value in.
@Message
The sentence a stored procedure hands back when it refuses to act. When it is blank, the action worked.
RETURN
Stop here: nothing below this line runs.
SCOPE_IDENTITY()
The number the database gave to the row that was added a moment ago.
IF EXISTS
A test that is true when the SELECT inside the brackets finds at least one row.
LIKE
A match on part of a piece of text, where % stands for any letters at all.
JOIN
Lining up the rows of two tables where a number in one matches a number in the other, so names can be shown instead of numbers.
GO
A word for SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), not for the database: run everything above this line as one batch, then start a fresh one.
Variable
A named box that holds one value while a script runs, made with DECLARE and filled with SET.
Batch
A group of lines that SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) sends to the database together.

blocks.p: Every stored procedure in this guide is named the same way: usp, an underscore, the table it works on, an underscore, and what it does. usp_Customer_Search searches the Customer table. usp_Customer_Delete deletes from it. The usp at the front stands for user stored procedure, and it keeps your own ones apart from the ones the database comes with. When SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) lists them, every Customer one sits beside the others, which makes them easy to find.

There are four shapes, and you will meet each one in turn. A Get fetches rows and changes nothing. An Add puts one row in and hands back its new number. An Update changes one row. A Delete takes one row out, and checks first. Each shape is the same from table to table, so once you have written one Add, you can write every Add.

screens.title: Copy the customer search into your script, and run the whole script once.

blocks.p: The first stored procedure searches for customers. The program's customers screen in chapter 6 will have a search box, and whatever is typed in it goes into this stored procedure as @SearchText. Any customer whose first name, last name or phone number contains that text comes back, in surname order. Read every part, then paste it in.

code.title: usp_Customer_Search: find customers by part of a name or phone number
parts: The name, and what goes in

CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE makes a stored procedure with this name, or replaces the one already there, so the script can run again and again. The one parameter is @SearchText, up to 50 characters of text. A parameter is an ingredient the stored procedure needs, and its name always starts with @.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.

Each row that comes back has the customer's number, their first and last names joined with a space into one column called FullName, their phone, their email and the day they joined. AS gives the joined column its name.
The rows come from the Customer table, and from nowhere else.

LIKE matches part of a piece of text. The % signs stand for any letters at all, so '%' + @SearchText + '%' means the search text anywhere inside. There are three tests joined by OR, so a customer comes back when the text is in their first name, or in their last name, or in their phone number.

The rows come back in order of surname, and two customers with the same surname are put in first-name order. END closes the work that BEGIN opened. GO is not SQL. It is a word for SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS): run everything above this line as one batch, then start a fresh one. Every stored procedure ends with its own GO.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Customer_Search
    @SearchText VARCHAR(50)
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT CustomerID,
           FirstName + ' ' + LastName AS FullName,
           Phone, Email, DateJoined
    FROM Customer
    WHERE FirstName LIKE '%' + @SearchText + '%'
       OR LastName  LIKE '%' + @SearchText + '%'
       OR Phone     LIKE '%' + @SearchText + '%'
    ORDER BY LastName, FirstName;
END
GO

code.title: usp_Customer_GetByID: one customer, by number
parts: The name, and what goes in
The one parameter is the customer's number, a whole number, which is what INT means.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.
What comes back, and from where
The SELECT takes six columns from the Customer table. The names stay in two columns this time, because the edit form in chapter 6 has a box for each.

The WHERE line keeps only the row whose number matches the parameter. A number is given to one row and never reused, so this is one row or none. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Customer_GetByID
    @CustomerID INT
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Phone, Email, DateJoined
    FROM Customer
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
END
GO

stages.title: The Add kind: a stored procedure that puts a row in

screens.title: Copy the stored procedure that adds a customer, and read the two things that come back out.

blocks.p: An Add puts one row into the table. Two things come back out of it. The first is the number the database chose for the new row, because the program will need it. The second is @Message, the one way a stored procedure says no. Every stored procedure that changes data has @Message as its last parameter. This one has no rule to check, so its message is always blank, and that blank is the sign that it worked.

code.title: usp_Customer_Add: put one customer in, and hand back the new number
parts: The name, and what goes in and out

Four parameters carry the customer's details in: first name, last name, phone and email, each with the same size as its column in the table. The last two have the word OUTPUT after them, which means they carry an answer back out: @NewCustomerID will hold the new number, and @Message the refusal, if there is one.
AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts. The first line of work makes @Message blank. A blank message is the sign that everything worked, so it must be blank before any check can change it.

INSERT INTO names the table and the four columns to fill. VALUES gives the four parameters, in the same order. CustomerID and DateJoined are not listed, because the table fills them itself: the next number, and today's date.

blocks.p: A stored procedure with OUTPUT parameters needs somewhere to put its answers. The test makes two variables, runs the stored procedure, and then looks at what came back. If the message is blank, it prints the new number. Then it fetches the new row with the stored procedure from the last stage, using that number.

screens.title: Type the lines that make an Update different from an Add.

blocks.p: An Update changes one row that is already there. It is the Add with two things changed: the customer's number comes in as well, so the stored procedure knows which row, and the INSERT becomes an UPDATE with a WHERE. Everything else is the same, so this one is pasted with a gap, and you type the four lines that differ.

code.title: usp_Customer_Update: change one customer
parts: The name, and what goes in and out
The customer's number comes first, then the same four details as the Add. @Message comes back out. There is no new number to hand back, because the row already has one.
AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts. The first line of work makes @Message blank. A blank message is the sign that everything worked, so it must be blank before any check can change it.

UPDATE names the table. SET gives each column its new value from the matching parameter, with commas between. WHERE picks the one row whose number matches, and without it every customer would get these details. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.why: UPDATE without a WHERE changes every row in the table. Typing the WHERE yourself, once, is the best way to never forget it.

screens.title: Copy the stored procedure that lists a customer's bookings with names in it.

blocks.p: A booking row holds numbers: the mechanic is 4, the service is 4. Nobody in the shop knows who 4 is. A Get that shows bookings has to swap each number for the name it stands for, and JOIN is how. JOIN lines up the rows of two tables where a number in one matches a number in the other. This stored procedure joins the bookings to Staff for the mechanic's name and to ServiceType for the service's name. The customers screen in chapter 6 will show its rows in a grid.

code.title: usp_Appointment_GetForCustomer: one customer's bookings, with names
parts: The name, and what goes in
The one parameter is the customer's number.
This stored procedure only reads, so it has no @Message. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.

Each column has a short letter and a dot in front, which says which table it comes from: a for Appointment, m for the mechanic's row in Staff, st for ServiceType. The mechanic's two names are joined into one column called Mechanic, and the service's name is called Service. The booking's own columns come as they are.
The rows start from the Appointment table. The a after the table name is the short letter the SELECT used, and it saves typing the whole word each time.
Two joins: the mechanic and the service

The first JOIN lines up each booking with the Staff row whose StaffID matches the booking's MechanicID, and calls it m. The second lines up each booking with the ServiceType row whose number matches, and calls it st. ON says which numbers must match. After the joins, every name is within reach.
The WHERE line keeps only the bookings whose customer number matches the parameter.
DESC means descending, so the latest booking is at the top of the list. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Appointment_GetForCustomer
    @CustomerID INT
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT a.AppointmentID, a.StartTime, a.EndTime,
           m.FirstName + ' ' + m.LastName AS Mechanic,
           st.Name AS Service, st.Price, a.BikeDescription, a.Status
    FROM Appointment a
    JOIN Staff       m  ON m.StaffID        = a.MechanicID
    JOIN ServiceType st ON st.ServiceTypeID = a.ServiceTypeID
    WHERE a.CustomerID = @CustomerID
    ORDER BY a.StartTime DESC;
END
GO

CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Staff_GetMechanics
AS
BEGIN

    FROM Staff
    WHERE Role = 'Mechanic' AND IsActive = 1
    ORDER BY FirstName, LastName;

GO

parts: There are no parameters, because every service is wanted. AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts.

The SELECT brings back the four columns of the table, then Display, which is built from three of them. CAST turns a number into text so that it can be joined on with plus signs. VARCHAR(5) is room for up to five characters of minutes. The pound sign is typed as it is, inside the quotes.

code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_ServiceType_GetAll
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT ServiceTypeID, Name, DurationMinutes, Price,
           Name + ' (' + CAST(DurationMinutes AS VARCHAR(5)) + ' min, £'
               + CAST(Price AS VARCHAR) + ')' AS Display
    FROM ServiceType
    ORDER BY DurationMinutes, Name;
END
GO

box.title: Make it yours
box.text: Your scenario has its own tables, and most tables need four stored procedures: a Get, an Add, an Update and a Delete. A table that other tables point at, such as a customer with bookings, needs a Delete that refuses. For each table, write down which of the four it needs. Then write one plain sentence for the rule each Add or Delete checks before it acts, because that sentence is what goes into @Message. Name each stored procedure with usp, then the table, then the action, for example usp_Customer_Add. In every Add, Update and Delete, set @Message to a blank message first and use RETURN after a refusal. In every Add, hand back SCOPE_IDENTITY().
